scenes.tts: In 1943, in St. Louis, Carl and Gerty Cori and their colleague Arda Green crystallized glycogen phosphorylase. It is the muscle enzyme that releases glucose units from glycogen. They found it in two forms. Phosphorylase a was active alone. Phosphorylase b worked only when A M P was present.
scenes.caption: In 1943, in St. Louis, Carl and Gerty Cori and their colleague Arda Green crystallized glycogen phosphorylase. It is the muscle enzyme that releases glucose units from glycogen. They found it in two forms. Phosphorylase a was active alone. Phosphorylase b worked only when AMP was present.
scenes.visual: One enzyme made of two chains splits into form a, lit as active alone, and form b, dark until an AMP chip docks on it.
scenes.narration: In 1943, in St. Louis, Carl and Gerty Cori and their colleague Arda Green crystallized glycogen phosphorylase. It is the muscle enzyme that releases glucose units from glycogen. They found it in two forms. Phosphorylase a was active alone. Phosphorylase b worked only when AMP was present.

scenes.tts: The Cori team also had an enzyme that turned a into b. They assumed it clipped off a bound A M P. That was not so. It was in fact a phosphatase. So what did separate a from b?
scenes.caption: The Cori team also had an enzyme that turned a into b. They assumed it clipped off a bound AMP. That was not so. It was in fact a phosphatase. So what did separate a from b?
scenes.visual: An enzyme chip sits on the arrow from a to b. The Coris' assumption, an AMP chip clipped off, appears dashed, then is crossed out and the enzyme is relabelled phosphatase.
scenes.narration: The Cori team also had an enzyme that turned a into b. They assumed it clipped off a bound AMP. That was not so. It was in fact a phosphatase. So what did separate a from b?

scenes.tts: In 1955, in Seattle, Edmond Fischer and Edwin Krebs tried to make phosphorylase a by the Cori recipe. They kept getting b, unless they filtered the extract through paper. The paper was leaching calcium, and extracts left standing ran out of A T P.
scenes.caption: In 1955, in Seattle, Edmond Fischer and Edwin Krebs tried to make phosphorylase a by the Cori recipe. They kept getting b, unless they filtered the extract through paper. The paper was leaching calcium, and extracts left standing ran out of ATP.
scenes.visual: An extract goes through the Cori recipe and comes out b where a was wanted. With a paper filter in the path it comes out a. Calcium drips off the paper; a second extract left standing loses its ATP chip.
scenes.narration: In 1955, in Seattle, Edmond Fischer and Edwin Krebs tried to make phosphorylase a by the Cori recipe. They kept getting b, unless they filtered the extract through paper. The paper was leaching calcium, and extracts left standing ran out of ATP.

scenes.tts: Over the next few years, the conversion of b to a proved to be an enzyme transferring one phosphate from A T P to one serine on each chain of the enzyme. So a carries the phosphate, and b does not. A phosphate, added by one enzyme and removed by another, was the switch.
scenes.caption: Over the next few years, the conversion of b to a proved to be an enzyme transferring one phosphate from ATP to one serine on each chain of the enzyme. So a carries the phosphate, and b does not. A phosphate, added by one enzyme and removed by another, was the switch.
scenes.visual: Form b with an enzyme and an ATP chip; one phosphate lands on a serine marker on each chain and the enzyme lights as a. Then a return arrow, the phosphatase, takes it back to b.
scenes.narration: Over the next few years, the conversion of b to a proved to be an enzyme transferring one phosphate from ATP to one serine on each chain of the enzyme. So a carries the phosphate, and b does not. A phosphate, added by one enzyme and removed by another, was the switch.
